meta.title: IBM AI-First Transformation Playbook
meta.subtitle: You've been asked to transform a workflow with AI. Everything you need to do it is here.
meta.footerText: Created by Claire Liu and Alexandra Ko 2026

endToEndWorkflow.title: End-to-End Workflow
endToEndWorkflow.description: Open Engage, Discover, and Execute to see workflow steps, key activities, readiness checklists, deliverables, modules, and pitfalls.

nodes.label: Technology & Data Foundations Assessment
nodes.subtext: Establish baseline of technology and data AI-readiness. Confirm sponsorship, team structure, and go/no-go before committing to workflow analysis.

nodes.label: Business Process Mapping
nodes.subtext: Define business processes and associated value to determine where to focus. Identify candidate workflows and build the business case.

nodes.label: Workflow Analysis
nodes.subtext: Analyze domain-specific workflows to identify highest-impact opportunities. Score and prioritize candidates, select MVP target, lock metrics and baselines.

nodes.label: Solution Design
nodes.subtext: Align on problem statement and design blank-slate AI solution. Define MVP scope, create build-ready requirements, prepare for build kickoff.

nodes.label: Experimentation
nodes.subtext: Rapidly deploy MVP, iterate in 2-week sprint cycles, measure impact against baselines. Track value throughout the build — not just at the end.

nodes.label: Scale & Adopt
nodes.subtext: Implement solution into live workflows, monitor for improvement, drive AI-first mindset. Hand off ownership and plan the next workflow.

phaseGroups.name: Engage
phaseGroups.description: Confirm readiness, value sponsorship, staffing, governance, and feasibility before detailed design or build.

steps.name: Assess
steps.briefDescription: Determine domain readiness, secure sponsorship, establish team structure, and make go/no-go decision before committing to detailed workflow analysis.
steps.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when you've taken an honest read on the domain's readiness and data, confirmed an executive sponsor, stood up the team and governance, and made a clear go/no-go decision to proceed.

keyActivities.title: Conduct current-state assessment
keyActivities.description: Gather people, process, technology, data, policies, roles, operating model context, and in-flight transformations. Understand the domain context, constraints, and readiness baseline to determine if transformation is feasible and where to focus initial efforts.

keyActivities.title: Conduct user interviews to map the process
keyActivities.description: Interview end users and process owners to understand current workflows, pain points, and opportunities. Document the as-is process through firsthand user insights to identify automation and improvement opportunities.

keyActivities.title: Identify high-level pain points and opportunities
keyActivities.description: Capture where work is slow, manual, costly, fragmented, risky, low quality, or difficult to scale at a domain level. Build initial business case and identify candidate areas for deeper workflow analysis without diving into detailed process mapping yet.

keyActivities.title: Evaluate data readiness
keyActivities.description: Confirm required data exists, is accessible, owned, trusted, and usable for AI-enabled transformation. Identify data gaps early to avoid downstream delays and ensure AI solutions can be built on reliable, accessible data.

keyActivities.title: Gather technology architecture blueprints
keyActivities.description: Identify systems of record, platforms, integrations, APIs, access constraints, ARB needs, and technical owners. Understand technical constraints and integration complexity to scope realistic solutions and avoid architecture surprises during build.

keyActivities.title: Align stakeholders and executive sponsors
keyActivities.description: Confirm sponsor air cover, domain focal, project lead, CIO/BPT/TPT involvement, Finance/EBM support, and decision rights. Secure executive air cover and decision rights to unblock issues quickly and ensure the transformation has organizational support to succeed.

keyActivities.title: Set up initial governance and RAID
keyActivities.description: Create governance structure, RACI, steering forum, escalation path, and RAID log before the sprint clock starts. Establish clear accountability and escalation paths to resolve blockers quickly and maintain momentum throughout the transformation.

keyActivities.title: Make go/no-go decision
keyActivities.description: Review readiness assessment, sponsorship commitment, team availability, data/tech feasibility, and value hypothesis to decide whether to proceed to detailed workflow analysis. Ensure all prerequisites are met before investing in detailed Analyze phase work, avoiding wasted effort on unprepared domains.

deliverables.title: Current State Assessment
deliverables.description: Captures the domain's people, process, technology, data, operating model, pain points, and readiness baseline. The honest "where we are today" snapshot.

deliverables.title: Business Case Template
deliverables.description: Quantifies the value case tied to the balance sheet or G&A: baseline, target, investment, and ROI.

deliverables.title: Technology & Data Readiness Checklist
deliverables.description: Confirms systems, data sources, owners, quality, access, architecture, and security constraints. Functions as a go/no-go gate before committing.

deliverables.title: Project Charter
deliverables.description: A one-page agreement that scopes the transformation before kickoff: the mandate, value target, sponsor, team, timeline, and sign-off. If you can't complete it, you're not ready to start.

deliverables.title: Business Process Map
deliverables.description: Documents the current-state workflow: handoffs, systems, users, bottlenecks, and automation opportunities.

deliverables.title: Staffing/RACI Matrix
deliverables.description: Clarifies who does what across sponsor, domain focal, PM, product owner, architect, developers, change owner, and value owner — one Accountable per activity.

deliverables.title: RAID Log
deliverables.description: Tracks risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies throughout the transformation. Reviewed at every steering committee.

phaseGroups.name: Discover
phaseGroups.description: Plan the AI solution for the chosen workflow: design the future-state, write build-ready requirements, scope the MVP, and set the roadmap.

steps.name: Analyze
steps.briefDescription: Deep-dive into workflows to map current state, identify bottlenecks, prioritize opportunities, and determine which specific workflows to transform. This phase ends when the target workflows are selected and validated.
steps.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when you've mapped the current workflows, chosen the one (or few) to transform with an evidence-based rationale, set initial value targets, and secured executive approval to proceed.

keyActivities.title: Identify opportunity areas
keyActivities.description: Work with business stakeholders and end users to identify opportunity areas, capturing executive-level priorities alongside frontline user research to surface real friction points. Surface genuine business problems and opportunities by combining top-down executive priorities with bottom-up user pain points.

keyActivities.title: Discuss peer and industry benchmarking
keyActivities.description: Benchmark from peers and industry best practices to define target workflow performance. Establish realistic performance targets and identify proven approaches by learning from industry leaders and best practices.

keyActivities.title: Map current business processes and document As-Is data
keyActivities.description: Create detailed As-Is process mapping documenting workflow steps, handoffs, user roles, systems, decisions, pain points, manual work, cycle time, volume, and quality issues. Document detailed systems, applications, data flows, and integration points in the current state. Create comprehensive process maps that reveal bottlenecks, manual work, handoffs, and automation opportunities to guide solution design.

keyActivities.title: Assess EIW alignment and automation level
keyActivities.description: Map to Enterprise Intelligent Workflow (EIW) and assess current level of automation down to level 3 processes. Align transformation to enterprise architecture standards and identify automation gaps at a granular process level.

keyActivities.title: Define initial outcome targets
keyActivities.description: Define high-level view of productivity improvements or growth expected from AI solution implementation with baseline metrics. Establish clear, quantifiable value targets tied to productivity gains or revenue growth that can be tracked throughout the transformation.

keyActivities.title: Prioritize workflows for transformation
keyActivities.description: Evaluate candidate workflows by impact, feasibility, data readiness, technical complexity, user adoption risk, and scale potential to select the transformation target. Make evidence-based decision on which specific workflow(s) to transform, ensuring resources focus on highest-value opportunities.

keyActivities.title: Define projected value and business case
keyActivities.description: Create a business case with projected value, expected benefits, and ROI for the selected workflow opportunity. Secure executive sponsorship and alignment by articulating clear financial targets and transformation vision for the selected workflow.

keyActivities.title: Obtain executive approval
keyActivities.description: Present selected workflow opportunity, high-level targets, and timelines for chairman/executive-level review and approval to proceed to Design phase. Obtain top-level executive air cover and commitment to ensure organizational support and resource allocation for the selected workflow.

deliverables.title: Opportunity Identification
deliverables.description: Documentation of opportunity areas identified through stakeholder interviews and user research, capturing both executive priorities and frontline friction points.

deliverables.title: External Benchmarking
deliverables.description: Benchmarking analysis from peers or industry best practices to define target workflow performance. Outside-in orientation to set realistic targets.

deliverables.title: As-Is Process Map (Inputs/Outputs)
deliverables.description: Detailed current-state process mapping documenting workflow steps, handoffs, systems, decisions, pain points, manual work, cycle time, and quality issues.

deliverables.title: As-Is Data/Architecture View
deliverables.description: Detailed systems, applications, data flows, and integration points in the current state.

deliverables.title: EIW Assessment & Automation Level
deliverables.description: Enterprise Intelligent Workflow mapping and assessment of current automation level down to level 3 processes.

deliverables.title: Initial Outcome View
deliverables.description: High-level view of productivity improvements or growth expected from AI solution implementation.

deliverables.title: AI Idea Brief
deliverables.description: High-level brief providing overview of opportunity, expected benefits/outcomes, and stakeholder alignment. Used to gauge interest from BU Executive and SVP sponsors.

deliverables.title: Chairman/Lesseps Review Deck
deliverables.description: Chairman-level review deck covering idea, opportunity, and high-level target timelines for executive approval.

steps.name: Design
steps.briefDescription: Design the AI-enabled solution for the selected workflow(s), define MVP scope, create build-ready requirements, establish team and governance, and prepare for build phase kickoff.
steps.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when the AI-first future-state is designed, the 90-day first version is scoped with build-ready requirements, the team and metrics are in place, and the kickoff has happened.

keyActivities.title: Develop future state process
keyActivities.description: Re-envision and standardize the future-state process for the selected workflow(s) including people, technology, and AI-enabled workflows. Create a blank-slate process design that reimagines how work gets done, not just automates the current state.

keyActivities.title: Buy vs Build assessment
keyActivities.description: Assess AI solutions available in the market versus building in-house. Consider cost, time, capabilities, and strategic fit. Make informed build-vs-buy decision based on market analysis, avoiding unnecessary custom development.

keyActivities.title: Build MVP strategic roadmap
keyActivities.description: Create MVP plan including architectural assessment, scope boundaries, and clear success criteria. Define a focused MVP that can be delivered in 90 days with measurable targets.

keyActivities.title: Build the RAID log
keyActivities.description: Create and maintain RAID log tracking risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies throughout the transformation. Surface and prioritize critical unknowns early so they can be addressed before significant investment.

keyActivities.title: Define operational and business metrics with baselines
keyActivities.description: Business defines operational metrics for the to-be process stage, aligned with AI Idea Brief. Include 90-day MVP metrics and baselines. Establish measurable targets with clear baselines that can be tracked through UAT and post-launch to prove value.

keyActivities.title: Build requirements log
keyActivities.description: Work with APPTIO EBM Team in CIO to enable automated tracking of MVP metrics through UAT. Break work into epics and features. Create build-ready requirements that development teams can execute against with clear acceptance criteria.

keyActivities.title: Get technical specification and solution architecture from the architect
keyActivities.description: Have the technical architect produce the tech spec and solution architecture (data objects, source systems, integrations, APIs, security/access constraints, and how the pieces fit together) alongside the business requirements. A build-ready technical blueprint the development team can execute against without guesswork, so the build doesn't stall on 'too conceptual to build from' requirements or hit architecture surprises mid-sprint.

keyActivities.title: Develop change management and adoption strategy
keyActivities.description: Plan users, UAT, communications, training, feedback loops, and resistance handling — started early, not at the end. Prepare organization for adoption by addressing people, process, and capability gaps before launch, not after.

keyActivities.title: Execute MVP Kick-Off
keyActivities.description: Align on 30-90 day roadmap, deliverables, ownership, and management system. Launch build phase with full team alignment. Launch build phase with full team alignment, clear ownership, and executive governance structure in place.

deliverables.title: To-Be Process/Experience Design (AI-First)
deliverables.description: Re-envisioned and standardized future-state process including people, technology, and AI-enabled workflows. Blank-slate design with an eye to scale.

deliverables.title: 90-Day MVP Plan with Hypothesis Testing Metrics
deliverables.description: Comprehensive MVP plan including architectural assessment, scope boundaries, riskiest assumptions, and metrics for validation.

deliverables.title: Riskiest Assumptions Test (RAT) Plan
deliverables.description: Force-ranked list of riskiest assumptions with test plans to validate them in the first 30 days of MVP execution.

deliverables.title: Operational & Business Metrics (with Baselines)
deliverables.description: Defined operational metrics for to-be process stage, aligned with AI Idea Brief, including 90-day MVP metrics and baselines.

deliverables.title: Buy vs. Make Assessment
deliverables.description: Assessment of AI solutions available in the market versus building in-house, considering cost, time, capabilities, and strategic fit.

deliverables.title: EPICs, Features & Requirements Documentation
deliverables.description: Build-ready requirements broken into epics and features with APPTIO EBM tracking enabled for automated MVP metrics monitoring.

deliverables.title: Cross-Functional Team & Resource MVP Plan
deliverables.description: Resourced MVP plan with roles, responsibilities, and commitments from CIO, business, and AIFT teams.

deliverables.title: Operational Cadences Plan
deliverables.description: Standup structure with workstreams to set weekly goals, remove impediments, align on messages, and execute demos and retrospectives.

deliverables.title: Discovery Package
deliverables.description: Aggregated package with all Discovery deliverables for stakeholder review and go/no-go decision.

deliverables.title: MVP Kick-Off Deck
deliverables.description: Alignment deck covering 30-90 day roadmap, deliverables, ownership, management system, and SteerCo cadence setup.

deliverables.title: Strategic Roadmap
deliverables.description: The roadmap for MVP, pilot, production, scale, backlog, dependencies, cadence, and next releases.

deliverables.title: Change Management Plan
deliverables.description: Plans users, UAT, communications, training, feedback loops, and resistance handling — started early, not at the end.

deliverables.title: SteerCo Charter
deliverables.description: Agenda, attendance, red/yellow/green norms, decision log, escalation rules, and governance structure for running the steering committee.

phaseGroups.name: Execute
phaseGroups.description: Build and experiment to prove feasibility (Build), then scale and sustain what works (Sustain).

steps.name: Build — Experimentation
steps.briefDescription: Rapidly deploy MVP with users and iterate with agile sprints. Test riskiest assumptions in first 30 days, then build and refine through 90-day cycles.
steps.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when the riskiest assumptions have been tested, real users have validated the solution, value has been measured against baseline, and you have a numbers-backed go/no-go to scale.

keyActivities.title: Execute 2-week iteration/demo/SteerCo cycle
keyActivities.description: A standing weekly or bi-weekly meeting with the executive sponsor and cross-functional leaders. Progress updates in roadmap (preferably in APPTIO 'on the glass'). A live demo of progress (working output, not status slides), metrics against baseline, top blockers needing executive help, key decisions to make, and a RAID/risk review — run with a 'red is good' norm so problems surface early. Maintain momentum and transparency through regular demos and progress tracking, keeping stakeholders aligned and engaged.

keyActivities.title: Plan and track MVP
keyActivities.description: Track progress 'on the glass' with focus on delivering MVP in 90 days. Monitor progress against roadmap, enabling data-driven decisions and course corrections.

keyActivities.title: Implement Change Management framework
keyActivities.description: Execute strategy to implement change at scale. Identify organizational, process, and talent gaps throughout build. Prepare organization for adoption by addressing people, process, and capability gaps before launch, not after.

keyActivities.title: Execute UAT Strategy and Planning
keyActivities.description: Address environments, data, approach, planning, resourcing, and tracking of user acceptance testing with real users. Validate solution with actual end users in realistic scenarios, surfacing issues and refinements before production.

keyActivities.title: Verify requirements
keyActivities.description: Go through the 90-day roadmap, MVP scope, and acceptance criteria and confirm every committed item is built, tested (UAT passed), and either done or formally de-scoped — nothing half-finished is being carried into production. A clear, evidence-backed confirmation that the MVP is genuinely finished against what was promised, so the scaling decision rests on a complete solution, not a partial one.

keyActivities.title: Confirm the metrics met their goals
keyActivities.description: Compare the operational and business metrics against the baselines and targets set in Design. Confirm the solution actually moved the numbers it was supposed to — and where it fell short, document by how much and why. An honest read on whether the solution performed to target, giving leadership the hard evidence (not enthusiasm) needed to decide whether to scale, adjust, or stop.

keyActivities.title: Validate that value was created
keyActivities.description: With finance/EBM, confirm the realized value against the original business case — real time saved, cost removed, or revenue gained from actual usage — and check it against the payback threshold set up front. A finance-confirmed go/no-go to scale, grounded in proven value against the payback bar, which is what justifies further investment.

keyActivities.title: Prepare Go/No-Go decision
keyActivities.description: Consolidate MVP performance data against target KPIs, financial and operational metrics, user feedback, and clear go/no-go recommendation with supporting rationale for scaling investment. Enable informed production decision with comprehensive evidence covering performance, value, readiness, and transition plan.

deliverables.title: 2-Week Iteration/Demo/SteerCo Deck
deliverables.description: Progress update deck showing roadmap status (preferably in APPTIO 'on the glass'), demos, and steering decisions on weekly or bi-weekly basis.

deliverables.title: 30-Day RAT Tracker (On the Glass)
deliverables.description: 'On the glass' progress tracking focused on validating riskiest assumptions in first 30 days, using APPTIO or similar tool.

deliverables.title: 30-Day RAT Debrief (Pivot/Continue/Stop)
deliverables.description: Assessment of riskiest assumptions test results and findings with clear recommendation to pivot, continue, or stop the MVP.

deliverables.title: Change Management Framework (Execution)
deliverables.description: Strategy implementation to drive change at scale, identifying organizational, process, and talent gaps throughout build.

deliverables.title: Metrics & Value Realization Framework
deliverables.description: Structured approach to quantify, track, and maximize business outcomes against baseline and targets throughout build.

deliverables.title: UAT Strategy & Planning
deliverables.description: Comprehensive UAT approach covering environments, data, planning, resourcing, and tracking of user acceptance testing with real users.

deliverables.title: Go/No-Go Decision Package
deliverables.description: Comprehensive package consolidating MVP performance against target KPIs, financial and operational metrics, user feedback, and clear go/no-go recommendation with supporting rationale for scaling investment. Includes role/responsibility transition plan and implementation roadmap.

deliverables.title: Production Readiness Packet
deliverables.description: Confirms requirements, UAT results, defects, limitations, support path, risks, and the go/no-go for scale.

steps.name: Sustain — Scale & Adopt
steps.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance (i.e. the transformation is durable) when the solution is in production with named owners, value is confirmed against baseline, adoption is holding, and the work has been handed to ongoing cadences.
steps.briefDescription: Implement solution into workflows, monitor adoption and value, complete graduation and ownership handoff, and manage continuous improvement.

keyActivities.title: Deploy production infrastructure
keyActivities.description: Production-deploy AI solutions integrated into target workflows with proper infrastructure, security, and monitoring. Ensure solution is running in production environment with enterprise-grade reliability, security, and performance.

keyActivities.title: Validate operational health dashboard
keyActivities.description: Track metrics and value realization using structured approach to quantify, track, and maximize business outcomes against baseline and targets. Provide evidence-based proof of value post-launch, enabling confident scaling decisions and ROI validation.

keyActivities.title: Align stakeholders on transition
keyActivities.description: Confirm all stakeholders understand their roles in the transition from AIFT/project team to business/CIO ownership. Create clear accountability and prevent gaps in ownership during the critical handoff period.

keyActivities.title: Transition back to BU (identify people with new R&R)
keyActivities.description: Identify specific individuals with new roles and responsibilities for business ownership, technical ownership, content/prompt maintenance, support, and value tracking. Ensure named individuals are ready and committed to sustain the solution long-term, not just organizational commitments.

keyActivities.title: Execute handoff and connect with ongoing cadences
keyActivities.description: Complete formal handoff with documentation, training, and connection to ongoing governance cadences (e.g., Kris Rose's team for continued support). Enable smooth transition with clear escalation paths, support channels, and governance integration for long-term success.

deliverables.title: Production Deployment Infrastructure
deliverables.description: Production-deployed AI solutions integrated into target workflows with proper infrastructure, security, monitoring, and enterprise-grade reliability.

deliverables.title: Stakeholder Alignment Plan
deliverables.description: Documentation of stakeholder roles, responsibilities, and commitments for the transition from project team to business/CIO ownership.

deliverables.title: Transition RACI & Named Owners
deliverables.description: Specific individuals identified with new roles and responsibilities for business ownership, technical ownership, content/prompt maintenance, support, and value tracking.

deliverables.title: Handoff Package & Ongoing Cadence Connection
deliverables.description: Complete handoff documentation, training materials, and connection to ongoing governance cadences for continued support and escalation.

deliverables.title: Graduation Checklist
deliverables.description: Confirms MVP acceptance, named owners, support model, telemetry, value tracking, and adoption plan before declaring graduation complete.

deliverables.title: Support & Maintenance Model
deliverables.description: Defines who maintains infrastructure, prompts, content, data, user support, technical health, and escalation paths for ongoing operations.

modules.title: Key Challenges
modules.description: Key Challenges are deep dives on pain points, organized by transformation workflow phase.

chapters.title: Value Measurement & ROI
chapters.definition: AI-first transformation value must be defined before the solution is built and validated after the solution is adopted. This chapter helps domain leads move from a high-level value hypothesis to a measurable business case, then from pilot evidence to realized value reporting. The goal is not to create a complex finance model; the goal is to define a simple, credible, repeatable way to prove whether the transformation improved the workflow.

phaseSections.description: Frame an initial value hypothesis and pick the benefit type before overbuilding any metric model.

actions.description: Select the value category (productivity, revenue, cost, risk) and draft a rough size of the prize. A directional value hypothesis that screens whether the opportunity is worth pursuing — without premature precision.
Identify a candidate baseline source and whether it can be measured meaningfully. Early warning on whether real measurement is even possible, so you avoid metrics you can't instrument later.

checklist: Value category selected (productivity, revenue, cost reduction, or risk mitigation)
Candidate baseline source identified and validated as accessible
Initial value hypothesis documented with rough size of prize
Finance/EBM partner identified for validation

artifacts.title: Business Case Template
artifacts.description: Quantifies the value case tied to the balance sheet or G&A: baseline, target, investment, and ROI.

artifacts.title: Measurement Strategy
artifacts.description: Defines baseline, target, source, owner, cadence, and validation method for each metric.

commonPitfalls: Building a complex metric model before the opportunity is even qualified
Picking a benefit you cannot measure in a meaningful way
Starting without measurable value hypothesis
phaseSections.whoToContact: Domain Finance/EBM partner for value framing

phaseSections.description: Lock the metrics and baselines before design — this is what the build optimizes toward.

actions.description: Define 3-5 leading metrics tied to the benefit type and capture the current baseline from source systems (not estimates). A measurable target the whole team aligns on before any solution is designed, preventing scope drift.

Decide how each metric will be captured — instrumented platform tracking preferred; surveys only as a weak fallback. A measurement approach that will survive executive scrutiny because it comes from a trusted, auditable source.

Where a tool is being replaced, set up an apples-to-apples before/after comparison of the same step inside the platform. Direct, credible evidence (e.g. "30 min in the new tool vs 90 min in the old one").

Pick a metric that matches what your project is actually meant to improve — time, money earned, or money saved. If the goal is saving time, you measure how much faster a task gets done (e.g. 90 minutes down to 30). If it's earning money, you measure real results like more sales closed or more customers signed up. If it's cutting costs, you measure money you no longer spend. This keeps you honest — you're proving real value, not just "people liked it."

Before building, agree how quickly the project needs to "pay for itself" — meaning the time, money, or savings it produces add up to more than it cost to build. Payback Threshold - A clear, objective bar for deciding later whether it's worth scaling. The common standard is that a solution should be on track to cover its own cost within about 12 months. Setting this up front means the scaling decision is based on numbers, not on whether the result "feels" successful.

Draft a lightweight business case that ties the project's savings to a real, hard number on the company's books — actual budget or overhead reduction, not a vague "efficiency" claim. A finance-approved business case that justifies the investment, because it's grounded in money the business can see on its balance sheet or in its operating costs.
Specify for each metric: name, baseline value, target value, source system, owner, and measurement cadence. Complete measurement strategy ready for implementation and tracking.

checklist: Business case ties directly to IBM's balance sheet or G&A reduction
Baseline metrics collected from source systems (not estimates)
Target metrics are specific, measurable, and time-bound
Finance or EBM has validated the measurement approach
Metric owners are assigned and committed
Measurement cadence is defined (weekly/monthly/quarterly)
3-5 leading indicators identified (not 20+ metrics)
commonPitfalls: Starting with soft benefits or cost avoidance instead of hard line savings
Using estimates instead of actual baseline data from source systems
Waiting until after the pilot to define metrics
Creating complex finance models instead of lightweight tracking
Not getting finance/EBM validation early
Defining too many metrics instead of focusing on 3-5 leading indicators
Relying on surveys because the platform isn't instrumented
Choosing metrics after the build, so you optimize for the wrong thing
Measuring 20 things instead of the 3-5 that matter

example.title: Speaker Agent Success
example.description: The MCC Event Speaker Agent team defined baseline metrics during the Analyze phase by measuring the current manual process: average time to identify and confirm speakers (5 days), number of back-and-forth emails (12 per event), and speaker confirmation rate (65%). They set clear targets: reduce time to 2 days, reduce emails to 3, increase confirmation rate to 85%. Finance validated the approach by confirming the metrics tied to G&A reduction through improved event planning efficiency. The team tracked these metrics weekly using a simple spreadsheet linked to their event management system.
example.contact: [Need to find transformation lead contact info]

phaseSections.whoToContact: Finance/EBM lead to bless the baseline and targets; value owner
phaseSections.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when 3–5 metrics, their baselines, their capture method, and a payback threshold are all agreed and signed off by finance.

phaseSections.description: Bake measurement into the solution design so value is tracked automatically, not retrofitted. Confirm reporting model matches MVP scope and value hypothesis.

actions.description: Specify the telemetry and instrumentation the MVP must capture for each metric. Auto-instrumentation built into the solution from day one, so value tracking doesn't depend on manual collection.
Confirm reporting model matches MVP scope and value hypothesis. Metrics updated to reflect any scope changes; reporting model drafted and ready.

checklist: Telemetry and instrumentation requirements specified for each metric
Metrics updated to reflect current MVP scope
Reporting model drafted and validated
Auto-capture mechanisms designed into solution architecture
commonPitfalls: Treating instrumentation as a post-launch add-on
Changing MVP scope without updating metrics
phaseSections.whoToContact: CIO/EBM team (e.g. Apptio) for automated metric tracking; value owner; Finance/EBM

phaseSections.stepSubtext: Track value against baseline throughout the build, not just at the end.
phaseSections.description: Track value against baseline throughout the build, not just at the end.

actions.description: Instrument the solution to automatically capture metrics (telemetry, usage tracking, EBM/Apptio integration). Auto-instrumentation built in from day one, enabling continuous value tracking without manual effort.
Track pilot metrics against baseline weekly during 2-week sprints. Continuous evidence of value that informs pivot/continue/stop decisions and de-risks the scaling case.
Adjust targets if baseline assumptions were wrong. Credible, realistic targets that maintain stakeholder confidence.

Don't wait for the tool to be polished — have real people use the early, rough version on their actual day-to-day work, and track how much time or effort it genuinely saves them. Real proof from real use, which is far more convincing than a projection or a guess. You can show "this actually saved 40 minutes per task in practice," not "we think it might help."
Document what's working and what's not for steering committee. Transparent value trajectory that enables informed decisions.

At the end of the trial period (about 90 days), make a clear recommendation — scale it up, change course, or stop — based on whether the results hit the payback target you set earlier. A keep-going-or-stop decision backed by real numbers instead of excitement. This discipline — only scaling what actually proved its value — is what separates the small minority of companies that get real returns from AI from the rest.

checklist: Solution has telemetry/instrumentation to auto-capture metrics
Pilot metrics are tracked weekly (not just at the end)
Early value signals are visible (even if targets not yet met)
Baseline assumptions have been validated or adjusted
Value evidence is ready for production readiness decision
Steering committee has visibility into value trajectory
Real users are using the MVP for actual work (not just testing)

example.title: Bob Agent ROI Validation
example.description: During the Build phase, the Bob Agent team instrumented the solution to automatically track usage, response time, and user satisfaction. They discovered that while usage was high (85% adoption), the time savings were lower than expected (20% vs. 40% target) because users were still manually validating Bob's outputs. The team surfaced this 'red' finding to the steering committee, adjusted the target to 25%, and added a confidence score feature to reduce manual validation. By the end of the pilot, they hit the adjusted target and had credible evidence for the production readiness decision.

However, they discovered that only 60% of eligible workflows had adopted the solution. They documented the lessons learned and scaled the pattern to 3 other manufacturing sites, multiplying the value impact.

chapters.title: Prioritization & Roadmap
chapters.definition: Select workflow opportunities, scope realistic MVPs, sequence delivery, and maintain a scalable roadmap. This chapter helps domain leads move from a broad set of AI possibilities to a focused, sequenced delivery plan. The goal is not to build a perfect long-term roadmap; the goal is to make smart decisions about what to build first, what to defer, and when to pivot based on learning.

phaseSections.description: Frame the opportunity landscape and confirm it's worth deeper analysis.

actions.description: Write one sentence describing the workflow's problem and roughly how much fixing it is worth. A clear, shareable framing that lets leadership sanity-check the opportunity before you spend time analyzing it. The rougher cost-of-the-problem number keeps you focused on workflows that are actually worth real money.

Collect candidate ideas through one organized intake, not scattered vendor pitches or pet projects. A clean list of real candidates tied to business goals, instead of a pile of "shiny AI" ideas that don't move the needle.
For each candidate, check whether a leader actually cares about it and will back it. Early confidence that a candidate is real — if no senior person will sponsor it, that's a sign to drop it now.

artifacts.title: Workflow Analysis Worksheet
artifacts.description: Analyzes bottlenecks, manual work, decisions, user pain, volume, cycle time, technical dependencies, and the AI opportunity for candidate workflows.

artifacts.title: Prioritization Matrix
artifacts.description: Ranks opportunities by value, feasibility, data readiness, urgency, user impact, and scale to select the MVP.

commonPitfalls: Starting from a solution ("let's build a chatbot") instead of a problem worth solving
Chasing an idea no leader has prioritized
Saying yes to too many projects at once
phaseSections.whoToContact: Domain executive sponsor for priority confirmation
phaseSections.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when you have a short, screened list of candidate workflows — each with a clear problem, a rough sense of its value, and a real sponsor.

phaseSections.description: Compare the candidate workflows the same way, pick the one to build first, and write down why.

actions.description: Rate every candidate the same way — a simple 1–5 score on how much value it creates, how doable it is, whether the data exists, how risky it is, how strong its sponsor is, and how easily you can measure it. A side-by-side ranking everyone can see and agree on — clear enough to defend to a finance leader or auditor. Scoring them all the same way stops the loudest voice from winning.

Set a few hard requirements (for example: the data exists, someone owns it, the risk is acceptable) and drop or rework any candidate that fails one, instead of scoring it anyway. A shortlist with no doomed projects in it — the ones missing essentials are filtered out before they waste budget.

Back up the top scores with real evidence — actual data samples, system records, process maps — not just opinions. Scores grounded in reality, which surfaces shaky assumptions and unclear ownership early, while they're cheap to fix.
Pick the one workflow to build first and write down why it beat the others. A decision you can stand behind later — and revisit if circumstances change.

artifacts.title: MVP Scope Worksheet
artifacts.description: Defines MVP boundaries: in-scope features, out-of-scope items, acceptance criteria, and assumptions.

artifacts.title: Strategic Roadmap
artifacts.description: The roadmap for MVP, pilot, production, scale, backlog, dependencies, cadence, and next releases.

commonPitfalls: Judging only on value and ignoring whether it's actually doable
Keeping a candidate that's missing essentials instead of cutting it
Picking the exciting idea over the one that's ready to go
phaseSections.whoToContact: Workflow SMEs for feasibility input; cross-functional scoring group
phaseSections.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when one workflow is chosen to build first, with a written reason it won, and the rest are parked or dropped.

phaseSections.description: Keep the first version small and focused, and map out the path from there to full scale.

actions.description: Spell out exactly what the first version will and won't do, and keep it as small as possible while still being useful. A focused, testable first version that protects your timeline.

List the assumptions that would sink the project if they're wrong, rank them, and plan to test the scariest ones first. The biggest unknowns get checked early — while there's still time and budget to react — instead of blowing up late.

Lay out a rough 12–18 week plan: easy wins first, harder bets later, noting what depends on what. A sequence that builds the team's confidence and credibility with quick wins before tackling the hard, risky work.

Favor building pieces you can reuse later — shared connections, components, and design patterns. Compounding value: build something once and reuse it across the next workflows, instead of starting from scratch each time.

artifacts.title: MVP Scope Worksheet
artifacts.description: Defines MVP boundaries: in-scope features, out-of-scope items, acceptance criteria, and assumptions.

artifacts.title: Strategic Roadmap
artifacts.description: The roadmap for MVP, pilot, production, scale, backlog, dependencies, cadence, and next releases.

commonPitfalls: Everything becomes "must have"
No clear list of what's left out
A plan that ignores what depends on what
Building from scratch when a proven option already exists
phaseSections.whoToContact: Product owner for scope; architect for feasibility

example.title: 📋 Example — Marketing (MCC): cutting scope was the right call
example.description:
A marketing domain team set out to transform a campaign workflow and initially scoped an ambitious AI agent to handle a large, complex piece of it. As they moved from the business vision into actual build requirements, the technical team kept hitting the same wall: the requirements were too conceptual to build from, and the target kept shifting as the business clarified what it wanted. Rather than push an under-defined, high-risk feature into the 90-day build and watch it slip, the team made a deliberate call to cut that agent from the first version and ship a smaller, well-defined scope they were confident they could deliver and measure.

The instructive part: leadership applauded the de-scope rather than treating it as a failure. It protected the timeline, kept the team focused on what was provably buildable, and left the ambitious piece on the backlog to revisit once the requirements were properly defined. The lesson for a domain leader: a smaller scope you can actually deliver beats a bigger one you can't — and naming that early, out loud, is a sign of a healthy transformation, not a weak one.

phaseSections.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when the first version is clearly scoped, the riskiest assumptions are ranked for testing, and you have a rough phased plan.

phaseSections.description: Hold scope during the build and de-scope intelligently when reality demands.

actions.description: Review scope each sprint against the timeline and make fast, documented de-scope calls. The core MVP stays protected and on-track even when capacity or dependencies slip.

commonPitfalls: Silently dropping features instead of formally de-scoping
Letting a slipping dependency sink the whole MVP

phaseSections.description: Plan the next releases so the transformation keeps compounding.

actions.description: Build the post-launch backlog and re-prioritize de-scoped items against new evidence. A living roadmap that turns one MVP into sustained, compounding value.

actions.description: Transfer the code repo (documented, with test cases), architecture diagram, secrets/API keys, and data documentation. A technical owner who can actually run and maintain the solution — not just a named owner on paper.

chapters.title: Adoption & Change
chapters.definition: Drive real usage and behavior change through user involvement, UAT, communications, enablement, and adoption tracking. This chapter helps domain leads move from building a solution to ensuring it's actually used and delivers value. The goal is not to deploy technology; the goal is to change how people work and prove that the new way is better. It's the challenge a domain leader personally owns, because adoption is 70% of the outcome and it's your people.

teamGuidance.title: ⚑ The Team You Need (for non-technical domain leaders)
teamGuidance.description: The hardest part of starting is assembling the team, because a marketing or finance leader doesn't have these roles on staff. Who to pull in, and from where:

roles.whatTheyDo: Owns outcomes, provides air cover, chairs the steering committee.
roles.whereToSource: You, or your boss — confirm before kickoff.

roles.whatTheyDo: Orchestrates the engagement day to day.
roles.whereToSource: From within your domain (often you or a trusted lieutenant).
Your domain — someone who knows the workflow deeply.

roles.whatTheyDo: Owns the tech spec, data pipeline, feasibility.
roles.whereToSource: Borrow from **IT / CIO org** — request early.

roles.whatTheyDo: Owns adoption, training, the staff transition.
roles.whereToSource: Your domain — a respected peer leader.

roles.whatTheyDo: Frontline experts who know the real workflow and pain.
roles.whereToSource: Your domain — the people doing the work today.

teamGuidance.upwardPitch: The upward pitch (to secure your sponsor): "We're transforming [one workflow] to [measurable outcome] in ~90 days. I need [named borrowed roles] and a weekly 45-minute steering slot to clear blockers. The ask is small; the proof point is a Client-Zero example we can scale." Keep it to one paragraph.

phaseSections.description: Begin change management at the start with a high-level impact read.

actions.description: Identify the main personas and, at a high level, whose roles change and how they may react. An early change-impact picture that shapes the solution and the adoption plan from day one.

commonPitfalls: Treating change management as a later, separate activity
Assuming technology alone will drive adoption
phaseSections.whoToContact: Change owner; domain sponsor for leadership alignment
phaseSections.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when you know who is affected and how, and change management is a funded, owned workstream.

phaseSections.description: Re-envision the future-state process, not just the technology, and get leaders excited.

actions.description: Analyze the current process deeply and re-envision the end-to-end future state (steps people take, not just the tech). A future-state the team can build adoption around — avoiding the late scramble of 'what will people actually do with this?'
Get leaders excited about the vision and the change. Top-down air cover that reinforces the bottom-up change effort.

artifacts.title: Change Management Plan
artifacts.description: Plans users, UAT, communications, training, feedback loops, and resistance handling — started early, not at the end.

commonPitfalls: Insufficient upfront process analysis — the R2A gap
Designing the tech without redesigning the work around it

phaseSections.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when the future-state process is re-envisioned and each affected role has a clear "what's in it for me," with visible leadership backing.

actions.description: Map stakeholders (champions/neutral/resistant), recruit real UAT users, and plan the communications arc. An adoption plan ready to execute, with the right users engaged from the first sprint.
Plan the learning & enablement approach and the old-process cutover. People know what's changing and what they need to do, and the old way is actively retired.

phaseSections.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when real test users are recruited, a training and cutover plan exists, and change is built into the delivery cadence.

phaseSections.description: Drive trust and real usage during the build through continuous user feedback.

actions.description: Get a small group to use the imperfect MVP for real work — start with one area, then expand. A mindset shift from 'wait for polish' to real usage, which compounds into voluntary adoption.
Manage communications and leadership alignment, demoing real progress to build excitement. Sustained momentum and trust as the solution matures sprint over sprint.

No support model, so the solution decays

phaseSections.readyToAdvance: You're ready to advance when every owner is named, the governance council and monitoring are live, and open risks are handed to the ongoing cadence.

caseStudy.title: Happy path example: A University Transforms Student Enrollment
caseStudy.subtitle: How a generic university applies the AIFT workflow to an enrollment and document-processing transformation — from identifying the opportunity to a scaled, sustained solution. Modeled on a widely cited higher-education AI transformation.
caseStudy.overview: This worked example follows a mid-sized public university — call it State University — as it transforms its student enrollment and document-verification workflow. It is a non-software, easy-to-follow scenario: a university drowning in manual admissions paperwork and inconsistent outreach. The journey is modeled on a renowned higher-education AI transformation and reconstructed step-by-step to mirror a real IBM-style engagement. Templates referenced in each phase are blank starting points — not filled-in samples — so you can adapt them to your own domain. Friction points are included to show how a real team works through obstacles.
caseStudy.startingContext: State University enrolls roughly 180,000 students across physical and online campuses. The enrollment team is overwhelmed: applications, transcripts, and required documents are processed by hand, creating bottlenecks that delay onboarding and frustrate prospective students. Outreach to prospects is scattershot — staff cannot tell which applicants are most likely to enroll, so effort is spread thin. University leadership has issued a mandate to modernize enrollment, but no specific AI use case has been chosen yet.
caseStudy.navInstruction: Click through each phase to follow State University's transformation step by step. Move as fast as you can through the steps without skipping them.

phases.mindset: Leadership wants us to modernize enrollment, but we don't yet know exactly what to build.
phases.summary: The team looks at the enrollment domain as a whole: confirms the mandate and sponsorship, stands up the team and governance, and takes an honest read on data and technology readiness before choosing a use case.
keyActions: Confirm the executive sponsor (VP of Enrollment) and secure air cover for the work.
Name the project lead and stand up a cross-functional team (operations, IT, institutional research, enrollment staff).
Run a current-state assessment of the enrollment domain: people, process, systems, data, and pain points.
Assess data readiness — are application, transcript, and interaction records accessible, owned, and usable?
Gather the technology and architecture picture: systems of record, integrations, access constraints.
Draft an initial business case tied to a measurable benefit (faster onboarding, staff hours saved).
Open the RAID log and set up the steering committee and RACI before any build.
Make a go/no-go decision on whether to proceed to detailed analysis.

sideways.issue: The sponsor wants to jump straight to 'build a chatbot for applicants.'
sideways.howHandled: The project lead reframes it: 'We're choosing the workflow opportunity first, not the tool. Let's confirm where the biggest, most feasible win is before committing to a build.' The sponsor agrees to a short Analyze phase with a decision gate.

takeaways: Don't start a build until the sponsor, project lead, technical owner, value owner, and change owner are named.
Use data readiness as a go/no-go input, not an afterthought.
Open the RAID log and stand up governance on day one.
Resist jumping to a solution before you understand the problem space.

phases.mindset: Which single enrollment workflow should we transform first, and why?
phases.summary: The team maps the candidate enrollment workflows, validates pain directly with counselors and applicants, benchmarks against peer institutions, and commits to one MVP target with a defensible rationale.
keyActions: Identify candidate workflows: document verification, application processing, prospect outreach, and transcript evaluation.
Interview enrollment counselors and review applicant feedback to find the real friction (outside-in).
Benchmark against peer universities to define what best-in-class enrollment performance looks like.
Map the current (as-is) process for each candidate, capturing cycle time, volume, and manual effort.
Score candidates on value, feasibility, data readiness, and adoption risk.
Select the MVP target — prospect outreach prioritization plus automated document verification — and document why it beat the alternatives.
Define baseline metrics and write an idea brief to secure executive approval to proceed.

sideways.issue: The most exciting idea — a fully conversational applicant assistant — turns out to depend on data the university doesn't cleanly hold yet.
sideways.howHandled: Feasibility scoring surfaces the data gap early. The team moves the conversational assistant to the backlog and selects outreach prioritization + document verification, which use data that already exists. Keeping the MVP small protects the timeline.

takeaways: Score opportunities by value AND feasibility, not excitement.
Validate pain with the frontline, not just leadership.
Pick the smallest useful MVP and write down why.
Define baseline metrics before you design anything.

phases.mindset: What exactly are we building for this workflow, and can we build it in 90 days?
phases.summary: The team designs the AI-enabled future-state for enrollment: re-envisions the workflow from the applicant's and counselor's perspective, writes build-ready requirements, scopes a 90-day MVP, sets the roadmap, and plans adoption from the start.
keyActions: Re-envision the future-state workflow: how an applicant's documents get verified and how counselors are directed to high-propensity prospects.
Decide build vs. buy for the underlying capability (e.g. partner platform vs. in-house).
Write build-ready requirements with data objects, source systems, owners, and acceptance criteria.
Scope the 90-day MVP — explicitly in (document verification + an enrollment-propensity model) and explicitly out (full conversational assistant).
Force-rank the riskiest assumptions and plan to test them in the first 30 days.
Confirm metrics and baselines with the value owner so the build optimizes for the right outcome.
Stand up the operating cadence (standups, steering committee) and plan adoption, UAT users, and training.
Run the MVP kickoff to align the team on the 90-day roadmap and ownership.

sideways.issue: The first requirements draft is too high-level for IT to build from — 'make outreach smarter' isn't actionable.
sideways.howHandled: The product owner and architect rework it into a build-ready package: the propensity model's inputs, the data sources, acceptance criteria, a fallback for low-confidence predictions, and the telemetry to capture. IT signs off on the second pass.

takeaways: Design around the applicant and counselor outcome, not the existing process.
Make requirements build-ready, not conceptual.
Test the riskiest assumptions first.
Plan adoption and recruit real UAT users before the build starts.

phases.mindset: Does it actually work — and can we prove it before we scale?
phases.summary: The team builds the MVP in sprints and experiments to prove feasibility. This is where data, platform, and integrations get stress-tested. Real counselors test it, value is measured against baseline, scope is protected by de-scoping, and a data-driven go/no-go decision is made.
keyActions: Run the first 30 days as a Riskiest Assumptions Test: can the model predict enrollment propensity accurately on real data?
Hold a 30-day debrief with the steering committee: pivot, continue, or stop.
Build the MVP in 2-week sprints with weekly demos to the steering committee.
Validate data quality on real application and interaction records — don't assume it.
Run UAT with real enrollment counselors, capturing result quality, satisfaction, and accuracy.
Track value against baseline throughout — verification time, outreach efficiency, onboarding speed.
De-scope lower-value features if needed to protect the core MVP and timeline.
Prepare the go/no-go package with performance evidence for the scaling decision.

sideways.issue: Early in the RAT, the enrollment-propensity model is barely better than guessing — data quality is worse than the readiness check suggested.
sideways.howHandled: The team assigns a data owner, documents the specific quality issues, and adds a data-validation and cleaning step to the pipeline. After the fix, the model becomes roughly four times more accurate than random — strong enough to continue.

sideways.issue: Counselors are hesitant to trust the model's prospect rankings and keep working their old way.
sideways.howHandled: The team adds explainability — why a prospect is ranked high, with the supporting signals — plus a feedback flag. Trust and usage climb in the next UAT round.

takeaways: Test the riskiest assumption (here, data quality) before investing in the full build.
Real-user UAT and explainability drive trust — and trust drives adoption.
Measure value against baseline continuously, not just at the end.
De-scoping to protect the core MVP is a success behavior, not a failure.

phases.mindset: How do we make sure this lasts and spreads after the project team leaves?
phases.summary: With the experiment proven, the team scales the solution and makes it durable: confirms named owners and a support model, validates realized value with finance, drives sustained adoption, and expands the pattern to more of the enrollment workflow.
keyActions: Complete the graduation checklist — the solution is ownership-ready, not just demo-complete.
Confirm named business, technical, content, and value owners for the long term.
Stand up production infrastructure with monitoring, security, and support.
Validate realized value with finance/institutional research against the original baseline.
Roll out training and enablement so counselors adopt the new workflow, and retire the old manual process.
Monitor adoption and intervene where it plateaus (office hours, champions, edge-case examples).
Start small, then expand: apply the proven pattern to additional enrollment areas and document types.
Capture the reusable pattern so other departments (financial aid, registrar) can adopt it.

sideways.issue: After launch, adoption plateaus — some counselors drift back to manual outreach because it's familiar.
sideways.howHandled: The change owner routes all new prospect lists through the AI-prioritized workflow, runs office hours, names counselor champions, and shares wins. Adoption climbs and holds as staff see the time savings firsthand.

takeaways: Graduation means a named owner, a support model, and value tracking — not just a working demo.
Validate realized value with finance so investment continues.
Start small and expand the proven pattern rather than boiling the ocean.
Capture the reusable pattern so the next department moves faster.
